1.1: On the day he became sick and knew that he would have to leave his body, he called his seven sons and his three daughters together and spoke to them as follows:
1.2: "Gather around me, children, and listen. I will tell you what 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 did for me and all that happened to me.
1.3: For I am Iyoḇ your father.
1.4: Know, my children, that you are the descendants of a chosen one, and remember your noble birth.
1.5: For I am of the sons of Ĕsaw. My brother is Naḥor, and your mother is Dinah. Through her I became your father.
1.6: For my first wife died a bitter death with my other ten children.
1.7: Listen now, children, and I will tell you what happened to me.
1.8: I was a very rich man living in the East in the land Ausitis, and before 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 had named me Iyoḇ, I was called Yoḇaḇ.
1.9: This is how my trial began.
1.10: Near my house there was an idol worshipped by the people, and I constantly saw burnt-offerings brought to him as an elohim.
1.11: Then I thought and said to myself: "Is this the one who made shamayim and earth, the sea and us all? How will I know the truth?"
1.12: That night, as I lay asleep, a voice came and called: "Yoḇaḇ! Yoḇaḇ! Get up, and I will tell you who it is that you wish to know.
1.13: The one to whom the people bring burnt-offerings and drink-offerings is not Elohim. This is the power and work of ha’Satan, by which he deceives the people."
1.14: When I heard this, I fell to the ground and bowed down, saying:
1.15: "O my master, who speaks for the deliverance of my soul, I ask you: if this is the idol of ha’Satan, please let me go and destroy it and purify this place.
1.16: For no one can forbid me to do this, since I am the meleḵ of this land. Then those who live in it will no longer be led astray."
1.17: The voice that spoke out of the flame answered me: "You can purify this place.
1.18: But listen: I will tell you what 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 commanded me to say to you. For I am the chief messenger of Elohim."
1.19: And I said: "I will listen to whatever is told to His servant."
1.20: The chief messenger said to me: "This is what 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 says: If you undertake to destroy and remove the image of ha’Satan, he will angrily wage war against you and turn all his malice against you.
1.21: He will bring many severe plagues upon you and take away all that you have.
1.22: He will take away your children and inflict many troubles upon you.
1.23: Then you must wrestle like an athlete and endure pain, certain of your reward, and overcome trials and suffering.
1.24: But if you endure, I will make your name renowned throughout all generations of the earth until the end of the world.
1.25: I will restore all that you had, and you will be given twice what you lose, so that you may know that Elohim shows no favoritism but gives good things to each person who deserves them.
1.26: This will also be given to you, and you will wear a crown of amaranth.
1.27: At the resurrection you will awaken to eternal life. Then you will know that 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 is just, true, and mighty."
1.28: Then, my children, I replied: "Out of love for Elohim, I will endure until death whatever comes upon me, and I will not shrink back."
1.29: Then the messenger put his seal upon me and left me.

10.1: Eliphaz and those with him were astonished at these things. They sat with me and answered me with boastful words about me for twenty-seven days.
10.2: They repeated again and again that I deserved to suffer because I had committed many sins and that no hope remained for me. But I answered these men, arguing vigorously myself.
10.3: They got up angrily, ready to leave in fury. But Elihu urged them to stay a little longer until he had shown them the explanation.
10.4: He said: "You have spent so many days allowing Iyoḇ to boast that he is just. I will no longer tolerate it.
10.5: From the beginning I kept weeping over him, remembering his former happiness. But now he boasts and arrogantly claims that his throne is in the shamayim.
10.6: So listen to me, and I will tell you why this has happened to him."
10.7: Then, filled with the spirit of ha’Satan, Elihu spoke harsh words, which are written in the records left by Elihu.
10.8: After he finished, Elohim appeared to me in a storm and clouds. He spoke, rebuking Elihu and showing me that the one who had spoken was not a man but a wild beast.
10.9: When Elohim had finished speaking to me, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 said to Eliphaz: "You and your friends have sinned because you have not spoken the truth about My servant Iyoḇ.
10.10: Therefore get up and have him bring a sin-offering for you so that your sins may be forgiven. If it were not for him, I would have destroyed you."
10.11: They brought me everything needed for a sacrifice. I took it and made a sin-offering for them, and 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 accepted it favorably and forgave their wrongdoing.
10.12: When Eliphaz, Baldad, and Sophar saw that Elohim had graciously pardoned their sin through His servant Iyoḇ, but had not chosen to pardon Elihu, Eliphaz began to sing a hymn. The others responded, and their soldiers joined in as they stood by the altar.
10.13: Eliphaz said: "Our sin has been removed, and our injustice is gone;
10.14: but Elihu, the evil one, will not be remembered among the living. His lamp has been extinguished and has lost its light.
10.15: The esteem of his lamp will speak for him, for he is a son of darkness, not of light.
10.16: The doorkeepers of the place of darkness will give him a share of their esteem and beauty. His Reign has vanished, his throne has decayed, and the honor of his stature is in Hades.
10.17: For he has loved the beauty of the serpent and the scales of the dragon; his gall and venom belong to the Northern One.
10.18: For he did not acknowledge that he belonged to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, nor did he fear Him, but he hated those whom He has chosen.
10.19: So Elohim forgot him, and the qodeshim abandoned him. His wrath and anger will bring him desolation, and he will have neither mercy in his heart nor peace, because the venom of an adder was on his tongue.
10.20: 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 is righteous, and His judgments are true. He shows no favoritism, for He judges everyone alike.
10.21: Look, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 is coming! Look, the qodeshim are ready! The crowns and prizes of the victors go before them!
10.22: Let the qodeshim rejoice and their hearts overflow with gladness, for they will receive the esteem kept for them. Chorus.
10.23: Our sins are forgiven, our injustice has been cleansed, but Elihu will not be remembered among the living."
10.24: After Eliphaz finished the hymn, we got up and returned to the city, each to the house where we lived.
10.25: The people held a feast for me in gratitude and delight in Elohim, and all my friends came back to me.
10.26: Everyone who had seen me in my former happiness asked: "What are those three things here among us?"

11.1: Wanting to resume my charitable work for the poor, I asked them:
11.2: "Each of you, give me a lamb to clothe the poor who are naked, and four drachmas of silver or gold."
11.3: Then 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 baraḵ all that remained to me. Within a few days I was rich again in merchandise, flocks, and everything I had lost. I received twice as much of everything.
11.4: Then I married your mother and became the father of you ten in place of the ten children who had died.
11.5: Now, my children, let me give you this warning: "I am dying. You will take my place.
11.6: Do not abandon 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄. Be generous to the poor, do not neglect the weak, and do not take wives from among foreigners.
11.7: Look, my children, I will divide my possessions among you, so that each may control their own share and have full freedom to do good with it."
11.8: After saying this, he brought all his goods and divided them among his seven sons, but gave none of his goods to his daughters.
11.9: They said to their father: "Our master and father, are we not your children too? Why do you not give us a share of your possessions?"
11.10: Iyoḇ said to his daughters: "Do not be angry, my daughters. I have not forgotten you. Look, I have kept something for you that is better than what your brothers received."
11.11: He called his daughter named Day and said: "Take this double ring used as a key, go to the treasury, and bring me the golden chest so that I may give you your inheritance."
11.12: She went and brought it to him. He opened it and took out three-stringed sashes whose appearance no one could describe.
11.13: They were not earthly work, but sparks of light from above flashed through them like rays of the sun.
11.14: He gave one string to each daughter and said: "Tie these around your waists so that they may encircle you all your lives and give you every good thing."
11.15: The other daughter, named Kassiah, said: "Is this the inheritance you say is better than our brothers’ share? What now? Can we live on this?"
11.16: Their father said: "You have more than enough here to live on. These also bring you into a better world to live in, in the shamayim.
11.17: Do you not know, my children, the value of these things? Listen: when 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 considered me worthy of His compassion and removed the diseases and worms from my body, He called me and handed me these three strings.
11.18: He said to me: ‘Get up and fasten your clothing around your waist like a man. I will question you, and you must answer Me.’
11.19: I took them and tied them around my waist. Immediately the worms and diseases left my body. My whole body received new strength through 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, and I went on as though I had never suffered.
11.20: In my heart, too, I forgot the pains. Then 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 spoke to me in His great power and showed me everything that had been and would be.
11.21: Now, my children, if you keep these, the enemy will not plot against you, nor will there be intentions in your mind, because this is a charm from 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
11.22: Get up and tie these around yourselves before I die, so that you may see the messengers come at my departure and look with wonder at the powers of Elohim."
11.23: Then the daughter named Day got up and tied the sash around herself. Immediately she left her body, as her father had said, and received a different heart, as though she had never cared for earthly things.
11.24: She sang angelic hymns in the voice of messengers and chanted angelic praise to Elohim while dancing.
11.25: Then the other daughter, named Kassia, put on the sash. Her heart was transformed so that she no longer wanted worldly things.
11.26: Her mouth spoke in the dialect of the rulers of the shamayim, and she sang a song of praise about the work of the High Place. Anyone who wishes to know the work of the shamayim may gain insight from Kassia’s hymns.
11.27: Then the other daughter, named Amalthea’s Horn, tied the sash around herself. Her mouth spoke in the language of those on high, for her heart was transformed and lifted above worldly things.
11.28: She spoke in the dialect of the keruḇim, singing praise to the Ruler of the cosmic powers and proclaiming their esteem.
11.29: Anyone who wishes to follow the traces of the "Esteem of the Father" will find them written in the Prayers of Amalthea’s Horn.

12.1: After the three daughters finished singing hymns, I, Naḥor, Iyoḇ’s brother, sat down beside him as he lay there.
12.2: I heard the marvelous things spoken by my brother’s three daughters, one after another, amid an awe-filled silence.
12.3: I wrote this book containing the hymns, except for the hymns and signs of the Word, for these were the great things of Elohim.
12.4: Iyoḇ lay sick on his couch, yet without pain or suffering, because the charm of the sash tied around him kept the pain from taking a strong hold of him.
12.5: After three days, Iyoḇ saw the qodesh messengers coming for his soul. He immediately got up, took the cithara, and gave it to his daughter Day.
12.6: He gave Kassia a censer, and Amalthea’s Horn a tambourine, so that they might baraḵ the qodesh messengers who came for his soul.
12.7: They took these, sang, played the psaltery, and praised and esteemed Elohim in the qodesh dialect.
12.8: After this, He who sits on the great chariot came and kissed Iyoḇ. His three daughters watched, but the others did not see it.
12.9: He took Iyoḇ’s soul and soared upward, taking her by the arm and carrying her on the chariot, and went toward the East.
12.10: His body was brought to the grave, while his three daughters walked ahead, wearing their sashes and singing hymns of praise to Elohim.
12.11: Then his brother Naḥor, his seven sons, the rest of the people, the poor, the orphans, and the weak mourned deeply for him, saying:
12.12: "How great is our sorrow! Today the strength of the weak, the light of the blind, and the father of the orphans has been taken from us.
12.13: The one who welcomed strangers, guided those who had gone astray, clothed the naked, and protected widows has been taken away. Who would not mourn for the man of Elohim!"
12.14: As they mourned in these various ways, they would not allow him to be placed in the grave.
12.15: After three days, however, he was finally laid in the grave as though in peaceful sleep. He was given the name of the good man who would remain renowned throughout all generations of the world.
12.16: He left seven sons and three daughters, and no daughters on earth were found to be as beautiful as Iyoḇ’s daughters.
12.17: Iyoḇ had formerly been named Yoḇaḇ, and 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 gave him the name Iyoḇ.
12.18: He had lived eighty-five years before his disease. After it, he received a double share of everything; his years were also doubled to 170 years. So he lived 255 years altogether.
12.19: He saw his descendants to the fourth generation. It is written that he will rise with those whom 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 will awaken again. To our 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 be esteem. Amĕn.

2.1: After this I got up in the night, took fifty slaves, went to the temple of the idol, and tore it down to the ground.
2.2: I went back to my house and ordered the door to be firmly locked, saying to my doorkeepers:
2.3: "If someone asks for me, do not report it to me. Tell him: ‘He is inside, attending to urgent matters.’"
2.4: Then ha’Satan disguised himself as a beggar and knocked heavily at the door, saying to the doorkeeper:
2.5: "Tell Iyoḇ that I want to meet him."
2.6: The doorkeeper came in and told me this, but I told her that I was studying.
2.7: When this failed, the Evil One went away, put an old, torn basket on his shoulder, and returned to speak to the doorkeeper, saying: "Tell Iyoḇ: ‘Give me bread from your hands so that I may eat.’"
2.8: When I heard this, I gave her burnt bread to give him and sent him this message: "Do not expect to eat my bread, for it is forbidden to you."
2.9: But the doorkeeper was ashamed to hand him the burnt, ashy bread. Since she did not know that he was ha’Satan, she took some of her own fine bread and gave it to him.
2.10: He took it and, knowing what had happened, said to the young woman: "Go, bad servant, and bring me the bread that was given to you to hand to me."
2.11: The servant cried and said in grief: "You speak the truth when you say that I am a bad servant, because I have not done as my master instructed me."
2.12: She went back, brought him the burnt bread, and said: "My master says: ‘You will not eat my bread anymore, for it is forbidden to you.’
2.13: He gave me this so that no one could accuse him of refusing to give to an enemy who asked."
2.14: When ha’Satan heard this, he sent the servant back to me, saying: "Just as you see this bread all burnt, I will soon burn your body and make it like this."
2.15: I replied: "Do what you want to do and carry out whatever you plot. For I am ready to endure whatever you bring upon me."
2.16: When the devil heard this, he left me and went up beneath the shamayim. He obtained an oath from 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 that he could have power over all my possessions.
2.17: After receiving this power, he went and immediately took away all my wealth.

3.1: For I had one hundred and thirty thousand sheep, and I set aside seven thousand of them to provide clothing for orphans, widows, the needy, and the sick.
3.2: I had a pack of eight hundred dogs that watched my sheep, and another two hundred to watch my house.
3.3: I had nine mills working for the whole city and ships to carry goods. I sent them into every city and village to the weak, the sick, and those in misfortune.
3.4: I had three hundred and forty thousand roaming donkeys. I set aside five hundred of them and ordered their offspring to be sold and the proceeds given to the poor and needy.
3.5: For the poor came from all the lands to meet me.
3.6: The four doors of my house were open, each under the care of a watchman who looked out for people coming to ask for help. If they saw me sitting at one door, they could leave through another, taking whatever they needed.
3.7: I also had thirty permanent tables kept ready at all hours for strangers alone, and twelve tables set for widows.
3.8: Anyone who came asking for help found food on my table and could take all they needed. I turned no one away from my door with an empty stomach.
3.9: I also had three thousand five hundred yokes of oxen. I selected five hundred of them for ploughing.
3.10: With these, those responsible for each field did all the work, and I set aside the income from their crops to provide food for the poor.
3.11: I also had fifty bakeries that supplied the table for the poor.
3.12: And I had slaves selected to serve them.
3.13: Some strangers who saw my goodwill also wished to serve as waiters themselves.
3.14: Others, in distress and unable to earn a living, came with this request:
3.15: "Please, since we too can serve as waiters and have no possessions, have pity on us and advance us money so that we can go to the great cities and sell merchandise.
3.16: We can give the surplus of our profits to help the poor and then repay what you lent us."
3.17: When I heard this, I was glad that they would accept this from me to support charitable work for the poor.
3.18: I willingly gave them what they wanted and accepted their written agreement, but I took no other security from them.
3.19: They went abroad and gave to the poor as much as their success allowed.
3.20: Often, however, some of their goods were lost on the road or at sea, or were stolen from them.
3.21: Then they would come and say: "Please be generous with us so that we can find a way to repay what we owe you."
3.22: When I heard this, I felt compassion for them and handed them their agreement. Often, after reading it aloud to them, I tore it up and released them from their debt, saying:
3.23: "What I have dedicated for the benefit of the poor, I will not take from you."
3.24: So I accepted nothing from my debtor.
3.25: When a man came to me with a cheerful heart and said: "I do not need to be compelled by wages to work for the poor,
3.26: but I wish to serve the needy at your table," he agreed to work and ate his share.
3.27: I gave him his wages nevertheless, and I went home rejoicing.
3.28: When he did not want to take them, I insisted, saying: "I know that you are a working man who looks forward to and waits for his wages, and you must take them."
3.29: I never delayed paying a hired worker or anyone else, nor kept the wages owed to him in my house for a single evening.
3.30: Those who milked the cows and ewes signaled to passersby to take their share.
3.31: The milk flowed so abundantly that it curdled into butter on the hills and beside the road. By the rocks and hills lay the cattle that had given birth.
3.32: My servants grew tired of keeping the meat for the widows and the poor and dividing it into small pieces.
3.33: They would curse and say: "If only we had some of his flesh to satisfy us!" although I was very kind to them.
3.34: I also had six harps and a cithara with ten strings, which I played during the day.
3.35: I took the cithara, and the widows responded after their meals.
3.36: With the musical instrument I reminded them of Elohim, so that they would give praise to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
3.37: When my female slaves complained, I took the musical instruments and played as much as they would have done for their wages, giving them relief from their labor and sighs.

4.1: After taking charge of the service, my children ate each day with their three sisters, beginning with the oldest brother, and held a feast.
4.2: I got up in the morning and offered fifty rams and nineteen sheep as a sin-offering for them. What remained was dedicated to the poor.
4.3: I said to them: "Take what remains and pray for my children.
4.4: Perhaps my sons have sinned before 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, saying in their pride: ‘We are children of this rich man. All these goods are ours. Why should we serve the poor?’
4.5: By speaking so proudly they may have provoked Elohim’s anger, for arrogant pride is an abomination before 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄."
4.6: So I brought oxen as offerings to the priest at the altar, saying: "May my children never think evil toward Elohim in their hearts."
4.7: While I lived this way, the Seducer could not bear to see the good and demanded permission from Elohim to wage war against me.
4.9: First he burnt up the great number of sheep, then the camels, then the cattle and all my herds. Others were captured, not only by enemies but also by people who had benefited from me.
4.10: The shepherds came and told me this.
4.11: But when I heard it, I praised Elohim and did not blaspheme.
4.12: When the Seducer learned of my endurance, he plotted new things against me.
4.13: He disguised himself as Meleḵ of Paras and besieged my city. After leading away everyone in it, he spoke to them with malice and boasting:
4.14: "This man Iyoḇ, who has obtained all the goods of the earth and left nothing for others, has destroyed and torn down the temple of elohim.
4.15: Therefore I will repay him for what he has done to the house of the great elohim.
4.16: Now come with me, and we will plunder everything left in his house."
4.17: They answered him: "He has seven sons and three daughters.
4.18: Be careful that they do not flee to other lands, become our tyrants, and then attack us by force and kill us."
4.19: He said: "Do not be afraid at all. I have destroyed his flocks and wealth by fire and captured the rest. Now I will kill his children."
4.20: After saying this, he went and brought the house down on my children and killed them.
4.21: When my fellow citizens saw that what he had said had come true, they came after me and robbed me of everything in my house.
4.22: I saw my house plundered with my own eyes. Uncivilized men without honor sat at my table and on my couches, and I could not protest against them.
4.23: For I was exhausted like a woman whose hips give way under many pains. Above all, I remembered that 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 had foretold this warfare to me through His messenger.
4.24: I became like someone who sees the rough sea and opposing winds and, because the ship is too heavily loaded in mid-ocean, throws the cargo into the sea, saying:
4.25: "I am willing to lose all this just to reach the city safely, so that I may keep the rescued ship and the best of my possessions."
4.26: This is how I managed my own affairs.
4.27: But another messenger came and told me of my children’s destruction, and I was shaken with terror.
4.28: I tore my clothes and said: "𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 has given, and 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 has taken. As 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 considered best, so it has happened. May the name of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 be baruḵ."

5.1: When ha’Satan saw that he could not drive me to despair, he asked 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 for power over my body so that he could afflict me with disease, for the Evil One could not bear my patience.
5.2: Then 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 delivered me into his hands to use my body as he wanted, but He gave him no power over my soul.
5.3: He came to me as I sat on my throne, still mourning my children.
5.4: He was like a great hurricane, overturning my throne and throwing me to the ground.
5.5: I lay on the floor for three hours, and he struck me with a severe disease from the top of my head to my toes.
5.6: I left the city in great terror and distress and sat on a dung heap, with worms eating my body.
5.7: The discharge from my sores wet the earth, for pus flowed from my body, and many worms covered it.
5.8: When a single worm crawled off my body, I put it back, saying: "Stay where you have been placed until He who sent you orders you elsewhere."
5.9: I endured this for seven years, sitting on a dung heap outside the city while afflicted with disease.
5.10: And I saw with my own eyes my longed-for children …
5.11: My wife had entered her bridal chamber in great luxury, with spearmen as bodyguards. Now I saw her humbled, working as a water carrier like a slave in a common man’s house to earn bread and bring it to me.
5.12: In my great suffering I said: "How can these boastful city rulers, whom I would not have considered equal to my shepherd dogs, now employ my wife as a servant!"
5.13: After this I took courage again.
5.14: But later they withheld even the bread she brought me, insisting that she should receive only enough for herself.
5.15: She took it and divided it between herself and me, saying sorrowfully: "How miserable I am! Now he can no longer feed on bread, and he cannot go to the market to ask the bread sellers for bread and bring it to me so that he may eat?"
5.16: When ha’Satan learned this, he disguised himself as a bread seller. My wife met him, seemingly by chance, and asked him for bread, thinking he really was a bread seller.
5.17: But ha’Satan said to her: "Pay me, and then take what you want."
5.18: She answered: "Where can I get money? Do you not know what misfortune has happened to me? If you have pity, show it to me. If not, you will see."
5.19: He replied: "If you did not deserve this misfortune, you would not have suffered all this.
5.20: Now, if you have no silver coin, give me the hair of your head and take three loaves of bread in exchange, so that you may both live on them for three days."
5.21: Then she said to herself: "What is the hair of my head compared with my starving husband?"
5.22: After thinking it over, she said to him: "Get up and cut off my hair."
5.23: He took a pair of scissors, cut off her hair in front of everyone, and gave her three loaves of bread.
5.24: She took them and brought them to me. Ha’Satan followed behind her on the road, keeping himself hidden and greatly troubling her heart.

6.1: Immediately my wife came near me, crying aloud and weeping, and said: "Iyoḇ! Iyoḇ! How long will you sit on the dung heap outside the city, still thinking and waiting for the deliverance you hope for?
6.2: I have been wandering from place to place, working as a hired servant. Look, your memory has already faded from the earth.
6.3: Have the sons and daughters I held against my chest, and all the labor and pain I endured, been for nothing?
6.4: You sit here, foul-smelling, covered with sores and worms, spending the nights in the cold air.
6.5: I have suffered every trial, trouble, and pain, day and night, until I managed to bring you bread.
6.6: They no longer allow me extra bread for you. I can barely take my own food and divide it between us, and I thought it was not right for you to suffer and go hungry for bread.
6.7: So I dared to go to the market without shame. When the bread seller told me, ‘Give me money, and you will have bread,’ I told him about our distress.
6.8: Then I heard him say: ‘If you have no money, give me the hair of your head and take three loaves of bread, so that you may both live on them for three days.’
6.9: I submitted to this wrong and said to him: ‘Get up and cut off my hair!’ He got up and shamefully cut off my hair with scissors in the marketplace while the crowd stood by in amazement.
6.10: Who would not be astonished and say: ‘Is this Sitis, the wife of Iyoḇ, who had fourteen curtains covering her inner sitting room and doors within doors, so that anyone allowed near her was greatly honored? Now look: she trades her hair for bread!
6.11: She had camels loaded with goods, which were taken to the poor in distant lands, and now she sells her hair for bread!
6.12: Look at her, who had seven permanent tables in her house where every poor person and stranger could eat, and now she sells her hair for bread!
6.13: Look at her, who had a basin of gold and silver for washing her feet, and now she walks on the ground and sells her hair for bread!
6.14: Look at her, who wore fine linen clothes interwoven with gold, and now she exchanges her hair for bread!
6.15: Look at her, who had couches of gold and silver, and now she sells her hair for bread!’
6.16: In short, Iyoḇ, after everything people have said to me, I now say this to you:
6.17: ‘My heart is so weak that it has crushed my bones. Get up, take these loaves of bread and enjoy them, then speak against 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and die!
6.18: For I too would trade the nourishment of my body for the numbness of death.’"
6.19: But I replied to her: "Look, I have endured this disease for seven years. I have endured the worms in my body, yet all these pains have not crushed my soul.
6.20: As for your words, ‘Speak against Elohim and die,’ I will endure with you the suffering you see. Let us endure the ruin of everything we have.
6.21: Yet you want us to speak against Elohim and exchange Him for the great Pluto.
6.22: Why do you not remember the great possessions we had? If these goods come from the lands of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, should we not also endure troubles and remain noble in spirit through everything until 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 again has mercy and shows us pity?
6.23: Do you not see the Seducer standing behind you, confusing your thoughts so that you will deceive me?"
6.24: He turned to ha’Satan and said: "Why do you not come openly to me? Stop hiding yourself, you wretched one.
6.25: Does the lion show his strength in a weasel cage? Does a bird fly in a basket? I tell you now: go away and wage your war against me."
6.26: Then he came out from behind my wife and stood before me, crying out: "Look, Iyoḇ, I yield to you, though you are only flesh and I am a spirit.
6.27: You are afflicted with disease, but I am in great trouble.
6.28: I am like a wrestler who, in single combat, has thrown down his opponent, covered him with dust, and broken every limb. Yet the one lying underneath shows his courage and shouts in triumph, declaring his own superiority.
6.29: So you, Iyoḇ, are underneath, stricken with disease and pain, yet you have won the wrestling match against me. Look, I yield to you."
6.30: Then he left me in shame.
6.31: Now, my children, keep your hearts firm through every trouble that happens to you, for firmness of heart is greater than all things.

7.1: At this time the melaḵim heard what had happened to me. Each came from his own land to visit and comfort me.
7.2: When they came near me, they cried aloud and each tore his clothes.
7.3: After bowing down with their heads to the ground, they sat beside me for seven days and seven nights without speaking a word.
7.4: There were four of them: Eliphaz, the meleḵ of Tĕman, Baldad, Sophar, and Elihu.
7.5: When they had sat down, they talked about what had happened to me.
7.6: The first time they had visited me, I had shown them my precious stones. They were astonished and said:
7.7: "If all the possessions of us three melaḵim were gathered together, they would not equal the precious stones of Yoḇaḇ’s reign. For you are of greater nobility than all the people of the East."
7.8: So when they now came to the land of Ausitis to visit me, they asked in the city: "Where is Yoḇaḇ, the ruler of this whole land?"
7.9: They were told about me: "He sits on the dung heap outside the city, for he has not entered the city for seven years."
7.10: They asked again about my possessions and were told everything that had happened to me.
7.11: When they learned this, they went out of the city with the inhabitants, and my fellow citizens pointed me out to them.
7.12: But they protested: "Surely this is not Yoḇaḇ."
7.13: While they hesitated, Eliphaz, the Meleḵ of Tĕman, said: "Come, let us go closer and see."
7.14: When they came near, I recognized them and wept deeply when I learned the purpose of their journey.
7.15: I threw earth on my head and shook my head, showing them that I was Iyoḇ.
7.16: When they saw me shake my head, they threw themselves to the ground, overcome with emotion.
7.17: While their armies stood around them, I saw the three melaḵim lie on the ground for three hours as though dead.
7.18: Then they got up and said to each other: "We cannot believe that this is Yoḇaḇ."
7.19: Finally, after seven days of asking about everything that had happened to me and searching for my flocks and other possessions, they said:
7.20: "Do we not know how many goods he sent to the surrounding cities and villages for the poor, besides everything he gave away in his own house? How could he have fallen into such ruin and misery?"
7.21: After the seven days, Elihu said to the melaḵim: "Come, let us go closer and examine him carefully to see whether he really is Yoḇaḇ."
7.22: They were less than half a mile from my foul-smelling body. They got up and came closer, carrying perfume in their hands, while their soldiers went with them and scattered fragrant incense around them so that they could approach me.
7.23: After spending three hours filling the path with fragrance, they came near.
7.24: Eliphaz began: "Are you really Iyoḇ, our fellow meleḵ? Are you the one who enjoyed such great esteem?
7.25: Are you the one who once shone like the sun by day over the whole earth? Are you the one who resembled the moon and stars shining throughout the night?"
7.26: I answered him: "I am." Then they all wept and mourned, singing a royal lament, with their whole army joining in the chorus.
7.27: Again Eliphaz said to me: "Are you the one who ordered seven thousand sheep to provide clothing for the poor? Where has the esteem of your throne gone?
7.28: Are you the one who ordered three thousand cattle to plough the fields for the poor? Where has your esteem gone?
7.29: Are you the one who had golden couches, and now you sit on a dung heap? Where has your esteem gone?
7.30: Are you the one who had sixty tables set for the poor? Are you the one who had censers made of precious stones for fine perfume, and now you are foul-smelling? Where has your esteem gone?
7.31: Are you the one who had golden lampstands set on silver stands, and now you must long for the natural light of the moon? Where has your esteem gone?
7.32: Are you the one who had ointment made from frankincense spices, and now you are repulsive? Where has your esteem gone?
7.33: Are you the one who mocked wrongdoers and sinners, and now you have become a laughingstock to everyone? Where has your esteem gone?"
7.34: After Eliphaz had cried and mourned for a long time, with everyone else joining in so that there was a great commotion, I said to them:
7.35: "Be silent, and I will show you my throne and the esteem of its splendor. My esteem will be everlasting.
7.36: The whole world will perish and its esteem will vanish. All who cling to it will remain below, but my throne is in the upper world, and its esteem and splendor will be at the right of the Savior in the shamayim.
7.37: My throne exists in the life of the qodeshim, and its esteem is in the imperishable world.
7.38: Rivers will dry up and their arrogance will sink into the depths of the abyss, but the streams of my land, where my throne stands, will not dry up. Their strength will remain unbroken.
7.39: Melaḵim perish and rulers vanish. Their esteem and pride are like a reflection in a mirror, but my Reign lasts forever and ever, and its esteem and beauty are in the chariot of my Father."

8.1: When I said this, Eliphaz became angry and said to the other friends: "Why have we come here with our armies to comfort him? Look, he rebukes us. Let us return to our countries.
8.2: This man sits here in misery, eaten by worms and in an unbearable state of decay, yet he challenges us, saying: ‘Reigns and their rulers will perish, but my Reign will last forever.’"
8.3: Then Eliphaz got up in great agitation and turned away from them in fury, saying: "I am leaving. We came to comfort him, but he declares war on us in front of our armies."
8.4: But Baldad took him by the hand and said: "You should not speak this way to a suffering man, especially one struck down by so many diseases.
8.5: Look, even though we are healthy, we did not dare approach him because of the offensive smell without plenty of fragrance to help us. But you, Eliphaz, have forgotten all this.
8.6: Let me speak plainly. Let us be generous and learn the cause. Could remembering his former happiness not drive him out of his mind?
8.7: Who would not be bewildered to see himself fall into such misfortune and disease? Let me go near him and find out why he is like this."
8.8: Baldad got up and approached me, saying: "Are you Iyoḇ? Is your heart still sound?"
8.9: I said: "I did not cling to earthly things, since the earth and all its inhabitants are unstable. But my heart holds fast to the shamayim, because there is no trouble there."
8.10: Then Baldad replied: "We know that the earth is unstable, for it changes with the seasons. Sometimes it is at peace and sometimes at war. But we hear that the shamayim are completely steady.
8.11: Are you truly calm? Let me ask you a question. When you answer my first question, I will ask a second. If you answer that clearly too, it will show that your heart has not lost its balance."
8.12: He said: "On what do you set your hope?" I said: "On the living Elohim."
8.13: He said to me: "Who took away everything you possessed? Who afflicted you with these diseases?" I said: "Elohim."
8.14: He said: "If you still place your hope in Elohim, how can He judge wrongly by bringing these diseases and misfortunes upon you and taking away all your possessions?
8.15: Since He has taken these, it is clear that He has given you nothing. No meleḵ will disgrace a soldier who has served him well as a bodyguard."
8.16: I answered: "Who understands the depths of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and His wisdom well enough to accuse Elohim of injustice?"
8.17: Baldad said: "Answer me this, Iyoḇ. Again I say to you: if your reasoning is sound, teach me, if you have wisdom.
8.18: Why do we see the sun rise in the East and set in the West, and then find it rising in the East again the next morning? Tell me what you think about this."
8.19: Then I said: "Why should I reveal the mighty mysteries of Elohim? Should my mouth go wrong by revealing things belonging to the Master? Never!
8.20: Who are we to pry into matters of the upper world when we are only flesh—indeed, earth and ashes?
8.21: So that you may know my heart is sound, listen to what I ask you:
8.22: Food passes through the stomach, and the water you drink through your mouth flows through the same throat. When the two go down to become waste, they separate again. Who causes this separation?"
8.23: Baldad said: "I do not know." I replied: "If you do not understand even the body’s outlets, how can you understand the circuits of the shamayim?"
8.24: Then Sophar replied: "We are not asking about our own affairs. We want to know whether your mind is sound, and we see that your reason has not been shaken.
8.25: What do you want us to do for you now? We have come here with the physicians of three melaḵim. If you wish, they can treat you."
8.26: But I answered: "My healing and restoration come from Elohim, the Maker of physicians."

9.1: While I was speaking, my wife Sitis came running, dressed in rags, from the service of the master who employed her as a slave. She had been forbidden to leave because the melaḵim might see her and take her captive.
9.2: When she arrived, she fell at their feet, crying: "Remember, Eliphaz and you other friends, how I once lived among you and how I have changed. Look at how I am dressed to meet you now."
9.3: Then the melaḵim burst into tears and were so deeply distressed that they kept silent. But Eliphaz took his purple cloak and put it around her so she could wrap herself in it.
9.4: She asked him: "Please, my masters, order your soldiers to dig among the ruins of our house, which fell on my children, so that their bones can be brought intact to the tombs.
9.5: Because of our misfortune we have no strength at all, but at least we could see their bones.
9.6: Do I have no more motherly feeling than a wild animal, that all ten of my children should perish in one day and I could not give even one of them a proper burial?"
9.7: The melaḵim ordered the ruins of my house to be dug up, but I forbade it, saying:
9.8: "Do not trouble yourselves in vain. My children will not be found, for they are in the care of their Maker and Ruler."
9.9: The melaḵim answered: "Who can deny that he is out of his mind and raving?
9.10: We want to recover his children’s bones, but he forbids us, saying: ‘They have been taken into the care of their Maker.’ Then prove this to us."
9.11: But I said to them: "Help me stand up." They lifted me, supporting my arms on both sides.
9.12: I stood upright and first praised Elohim. After the prayer I said to them: "Look toward the East."
9.13: They looked and saw my children wearing crowns near the esteem of the Meleḵ, the Ruler of shamayim.
9.14: When my wife Sitis saw this, she fell to the ground and bowed before Elohim, saying: "Now I know that 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 remembers me."
9.15: After she said this, evening came. She returned to the city, to the master she served as a slave, lay down at the cattle’s feeding trough, and died there from exhaustion.
9.16: When her tyrannical master searched for her and could not find her, he came to the cattle enclosure. There he saw her lying dead on the feeding trough, while all the animals around her cried out.
9.17: Everyone who saw her wept and mourned, and the cry spread throughout the whole city.
9.18: The people brought her down, wrapped her up, and buried her beside the house that had fallen on her children.
9.19: The poor of the city mourned deeply for her, saying: "Look at this Sitis, whose nobility and esteem no other woman equals. How sad that she was not considered worthy of a proper tomb!"
9.20: You will find the song of mourning for her in the record.
